newsitem.title: UK: UK funds remain negative on domestic shares - survey.
newsitem.headline: UK funds remain negative on domestic shares - survey.

text.p: British fund managers expect to be net sellers of domestic stocks in coming weeks but are keen buyers of gilts, according to a poll of 235 institutions for Merrill Lynch carried out by Gallup.

The survey, conducted between June 2 and 4, found that respondents had cut company earnings forecasts in the face of sterling strength and expected UK base rates to be pushed up through the coming year, prompting a negative view on equities.
Yet with the Bank of England given a free hand to set interest rates, managers had cut their forecasts for inflation and economic growth, underpinning their more positive view on gilts.

"Buyers (of gilts) in our survey outnumber sellers by 17 percent," said Merrill global strategist Bijal Shah. "The buying interest over the last two months has been the greatest since the first quarter of 1995."

The 17-percent balance indicates an only slightly less positive view than the 21 percent majority who expected to raise their gilt holdings in the last Merrill survey, in the immediate wake of the Bank being given indendence.
By comparison, a balance of three percent plan to cut their equity holdings, compared with a 12 percent balance in favour of reducing their holdings in the previous survey.

"Unlike continental Europe, the UK equity market is contending with the prospect of higher base rates and falling earnings per share forecasts," said Shah. "As a result we believe continental European equities will outperform UK equities."
The survey found that a balance of 14 percent expect UK shares to be lower on a three-month view, though a 33 percent majority expect gains on a 12-month view.

Forecasts for earnings-per-share growth for UK companies were cut to an average 8.5 percent from 8.7 percent, while the yield on the 15-year gilt was seen at 7.4 percent in 12 months, down from 7.6 percent.
The dollar remained favourite currency for the next 12 months, picked by 57 percent of fund mangers -- only slightly below last month's 63 percent vote.

The survey also found that UK fund managers swung to a negative view on continental European equities for the first time since January 1996, with a balance of seven percent planning to cut their exposure in the wake of the French election.
Germany swung to favourite market in continental Europe, replacing France.

Japanese equities remained in favour, with a 26 percent majority planning to raise their holdings, while a balance of 24 percent planned to reduce their cash holdings -- well up on the two percent who planned to run down cash last month.
UK property was in favour, with a net 19 percent planning to raise their investments.
